analysis.one_liner: Lets employers require workers to disclose medical and genetic information through workplace wellness programs.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill 22-17 and placed it on the House calendar in December 2017, but it never received a vote by the full House before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would allow employers to require workers to take medical exams, complete health risk assessments, and share family medical history as a condition of workplace wellness programs. It does this by exempting those programs from three federal laws that otherwise limit medical questioning of employees and the collection of genetic information: the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, and related health insurance rules. Employers could still attach rewards or penalties of up to 50% of insurance premiums to participation, as long as the program followed existing incentive limits and offered alternatives for people who cannot meet the standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that run wellness programs and the vendors that operate them. The bill removes the legal risk that a required medical exam, health questionnaire, or request for family medical history violates federal disability or genetic privacy law, making it easier to push workers into biometric screening and health questionnaires and to build premium-based rewards and penalties on top of that data.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts workplace wellness programs from Americans with Disabilities Act limits on medical examinations and inquiries of employees, from the ban on collecting genetic information when issuing health insurance, and from Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act limits on collecting genetic information about employees and their family members [S2][S3][S4].

Declares that collecting information about a family member's disease or disorder through a wellness program is not an unlawful acquisition of genetic information about other family members [S2][S3][S4].

Preserves the existing structure of rewards of up to 50% off insurance premiums for participation, as long as programs comply with Public Health Service Act incentive limits and offer reasonable alternative standards or waivers for employees who cannot meet the program's standard [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Workers, who would face a choice between submitting to medical exams, biometric screening, and health questionnaires covering themselves and their families, or paying more for health insurance. Because wellness program rewards and penalties can reach 50% of premiums, declining disclosure can mean a large paycheck cost, and the bill removes the disability and genetic privacy laws workers could otherwise sue under.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers who decline to disclose health data

drawbacks.text: The exemption strips away protections workers currently have under the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, leaving them no federal claim if an employer's wellness program demands medical or family genetic information they consider private [S2][S3][S4].

Participation can carry a cost of up to 50% of insurance premiums, so 'voluntary' programs with rewards that large put real financial pressure on employees to hand over health data, including about relatives' diseases [S4].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that wellness incentives can operate as penalties for people with chronic conditions, disabilities, or family medical histories, which is exactly why the disability and genetics protections existed; the bill addresses that only by requiring a reasonable alternative standard, not by limiting the data collection itself [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated benefit is clearer rules for employers who want to offer prevention programs and a preserved reward structure of up to 50% of premiums, with alternatives available for workers who cannot meet a standard [S4]. The cost falls entirely on workers' privacy: the bill overrides federal disability and genetic information protections so that participation-based medical questioning and family history collection carry no legal risk for employers [S2][S3]. The gains are procedural and flow to employers; the losses to employee privacy are concrete and broad, since most large employers run some form of wellness program.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Education and Workforce Committee on a 22-17 vote in March 2017, was reported to the House and placed on the House calendar in December 2017, and never received a vote by the full House before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 2017 by Rep. Virginia Foxx and referred to three committees [S1][S6].
On March 8, 2017, the Education and Workforce Committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 22-17 [S6].

On December 11, 2017, the committee reported the bill with an amendment (H. Rept. 115-459), the other two committees were discharged from further consideration, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, which is the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote [S1][S3][S6].
No further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died without a House floor vote and never reached the Senate [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept the existing Americans with Disabilities Act and Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act protections, since no law was changed. Employers and wellness vendors gained nothing new but also faced no new requirements, and House leaders who preferred not to take a politically difficult vote were spared one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who kept existing privacy protections

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and five Republican cosponsors [S1][S5]; in the committee's only vote it was approved 22-17, matching the committee's Republican majority against a unanimous-minority opposition, and the bill died without a floor vote [S6].

industries.note: These companies profit by running biometric screenings and health risk assessments for employers. The bill removes the legal risk that the data collection they perform violates disability or genetic privacy law, letting them reach more workers' medical and family data.

Employers gain immunity from ADA and GINA claims when they require medical exams and questionnaires and attach premium rewards or penalties up to 50% to the results. The gain comes at the cost of workers' health privacy and can mean higher premiums for workers who decline.

Insurers administering employer plans get a clearer legal basis for wellness-linked premium discounts and surcharges, which steer more health data through their plans and let them price premiums off screening results.
